title: Fear of man is acquired slowly by animals exposed to human persecution

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Fear of man is acquired slowly by animals exposed to human persecution

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Fear of humans is slowly acquired by animal populations persecuted by man, so animals on uninhabited islands are tame and heavily hunted large birds are wilder than small ones.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But fear of man is slowly acquired, as I have elsewhere shown, by various animals inhabiting desert islands

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VII, “Instinct”; section “Instincts variable”. Scope: birds and other animals on islands and in regions with differing histories of human persecution

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch07-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Many published observations make cross-population tests possible, but the key fear and persecution variables require substantial compilation. Causal acquisition speed remains difficult to isolate.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Relate flight-initiation distance or approach tolerance across populations to quantified duration and intensity of human persecution, controlling for body size, urbanization, and phylogeny. Increasing fear with exposure supports the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Urban habituation and species sorting confound persecution history.

Flight-initiation measurements are scattered rather than centrally standardized.

fields.value:

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A large public compilation of approach distances makes the island-tameness and body-size contrasts testable for birds, together with range and threat data. That is a proxy for acquired fear, not a measurement of the rate of acquisition or of heritability. Confounds are serious enough that a positive correlation would remain ambiguous, and non-bird scope is barely covered.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Regress flight-initiation distance on island isolation, history of human presence, hunting pressure, and body size. Longer distances where persecution has been longer or more intense, and shorter distances on uninhabited islands, would support the claim; no such pattern, or a pattern explained by predator fauna alone, would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The compilations are snapshots, so they do not measure the word 'slowly'.

Flight distance confounds evolved fear, individual learning, habitat, and the background predator community.

Geographic bias toward Europe, North America, and Australia leaves many persecution histories unsampled.
